scenario_name: Payment Contagion — Bank Run Breaks the Payment Chain
scenario_description: A high-credibility (false) rumor triggers a run on Redwood Regional Bank. The bank is fundamentally solvent but cannot pay everyone at once — a fast AI-speed run drains its reserves and forces a suspension. Treasurers can no longer make payroll; gig workers who counted on that income can't make rent; retiree landlords lose expected cash and run on their own deposits. The shock propagates through the payment graph, not just the news feed.

events.content: Multiple posts across financial social media claim Redwood Regional Bank cannot meet withdrawal requests. Anonymous accounts cite 'insider' sources. The posts are spreading rapidly but have not been verified by any news outlet.

A market-terminal alert cites two bank analysts and screenshots of a purported supervisory letter saying Redwood Regional Bank may miss its liquidity coverage requirement. The bank has delayed its investor call by two hours, and trading in its parent company's stock is unusually volatile.

What I'm actually holding here is $20k in rotation cash — not my emergency fund, not my core nest egg. I can absorb a full loss on this without materially changing my trajectory. The question isn't "can I lose it?" It's "what's the opportunity cost of my actions?"

The asymmetry here is real but not overwhelming — the cost of being wrong by holding (principal loss on $20k) is significant but not life-altering. The cost of being wrong by withdrawing (missing upside on fine cash, and feeling like I panic-sold) is moderate and reversible.

Split the difference. Pull half. De-risk the tail, but stay in the game in case this is noise. If real data drops in the next 24 hours — FDIC statements, Reuters, actual reporting, not posts — I can move the rest. This buys me optionality without committing to the panic narrative.
